the right STS is sensitive not only to biological motion but also to meaningful coherent motion in general, that it responds more strongly to the former than to the latter, and that the right STST is strongly lateralized.

the right lateralized superior temporal sulcus is sensitive to human biological motion, but that it responds more strongly to the perception of human walking than to the perception of a robot walking.
the human brain responds to biological motion with a complex pattern of activations and deactivations in multiple brain areas, with a strong right-lateralized focus in the STS.

the neural mechanisms underlying the perception of human walking.

the STS does not respond selectively to biological motion but responds selectively to coherent motion, and this response is modulated by the meaning of that motion.
STS activity is specific for biological motion and that this specificity is not simply due to the coherent and meaningful nature of the motion.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the STS, and perhaps the fusiform gyri as well, are selectively responsive to biological motion.

the STS, but not other regions, responds more strongly to meaningful biological motion than to nonbiological motion, even when the nonbiological motion is complex, coherent, and meaningful in its own right.
the STS, and other motion-related brain areas, are sensitive to biological motion, not just to complex or coherent motion.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the STS does respond more strongly to biological than to nonbiological motion, even when the latter motion is complex and meaningful.

the STS can be selectively activated by biological motion, and that this activation cannot be accounted for by the mere presence of moving elements in the display or by the presence of coherent, meaningful motion in the display.
